result: The authors developed a dual-cassette-donor strategy (PoNe donor) for one-step generation of dual-function knockin alleles in zebrafish. The donor contains a positive cassette (Po-cassette) designed to maintain target gene expression and include a fluorescent reporter, and a negative cassette (Ne-cassette) designed to disrupt gene expression after Cre-mediated excision through transcription termination signals and a mutated exon.
evaluation: Claims C4, C23, C24, and C30-C34 describe the design rationale and initial demonstration of the dual-cassette donor strategy. The methodological design is clearly articulated with supporting experimental data at tbx5a and kctd10 loci showing germline transmission efficiency up to 56% (C24). The Po-cassette and Ne-cassette designs are well-justified with appropriate molecular components.

result: LiCl purification of gRNA, particularly the gRNA targeting the donor plasmid (hEMX1 site), is critical for highly efficient knockin. Ethanol precipitation resulted in no fluorescent signal in injected embryos, while LiCl purification yielded >10% fluorescent embryos and successful germline transmission.
evaluation: Claims C7, C38-C43, C50-C51 present systematic experimental comparisons documented in Table 1 showing dramatic differences between purification methods. The data clearly demonstrate that LiCl purification of the donor-targeting gRNA is essential, with no germline transmission observed using ethanol precipitation (C50). The mechanistic speculation (C44) is appropriately qualified as requiring future investigation.

result: Preselection of F0 founders based on fluorescent reporter expression in embryos enables efficient germline recovery of knockin events. For tbx5a PoR-Ne, 5/9 (>50%) fluorescent-positive F0 fish transmitted KI alleles with mosaicism of 2.4-43.8%, while 0/40 fluorescent-negative founders showed germline transmission.
evaluation: Claims C8, C46-C49, C152-C154 present quantitative data demonstrating strong correlation between F0 fluorescence and germline transmission. The data in Supplementary file 3 support the high efficiency (>50%) in preselected founders versus 0% in non-fluorescent founders, establishing this as a reliable screening method.

result: The tbx5a PoR-Ne dual-function alleles display gene-tagging effects under normal conditions and conditional knockout effects after Cre induction. Without Cre, tbx5a expression is normal; after Cre injection, 25.6% of compound heterozygous embryos showed heart and fin defects, with tbx5a transcripts reduced ~15-fold in homozygous mutants.
evaluation: Claims C5, C25-C26, C59-C70 demonstrate both functions of the dual-cassette system with multiple lines of evidence: fluorescence imaging (C25, C52), phenotypic analysis (C59, C57-C58), genotyping (C61-C62), and qRT-PCR showing appropriate expression levels (C63-C64, C67-C69). The ~15-fold reduction in tbx5aNe/Ne mutants (C68) confirms efficient mutagenesis.

result: An improved geno-tagging strategy using dual fluorescent reporters enables conditional knockout coupled with fluorescent reporter switching at tbx5a locus. After Cre injection, 27.4% of embryos showed mutant phenotype with complete switch from tdTomato to tdGFP, and tbx5a transcripts were reduced ~12.5-fold in homozygous mutants.
evaluation: Claims C6, C27-C28, C87-C89, C97-C116 describe the geno-tagging advancement with comprehensive experimental validation. Complete fluorescent switching (C99), appropriate phenotype frequencies (C100), correlation between green fluorescence and defects (C101), mosaic analysis capability (C102-C105), and qRT-PCR confirmation of ~12.5-fold reduction (C113) all support the functionality of this system.

result: The geno-tagging strategy was successfully applied at the sox10 locus, demonstrating universality. Dual fluorescent reporters were detected in neural crest cells (29/126 embryos), 24.6% of Cre-injected embryos showed the expected colourless phenotype, and sox10 transcripts were reduced ~25-fold in homozygous mutants.
evaluation: Claims C29, C117, C122-C135 demonstrate successful application at a second locus with appropriate tissue-specific expression (neural crest cells), expected phenotype frequencies (24.6% matching Mendelian ratios), genotyping confirmation (C130), and strong mutagenesis efficiency (~25-fold reduction, C133). This validates the generalizability of the approach.

result: Dual-function KI alleles were generated at the kctd10 locus showing gene-tagging and CKO effects. Without preselection, 2/42 F0 (4.8%) showed germline transmission. After Cre injection, 25.9% of embryos from compound heterozygote crosses showed mutant phenotype, with kctd10 transcripts reduced to 0.3% in homozygous mutants.
evaluation: Claims C71-C83 demonstrate successful application at kctd10 with maternal expression confirmation (C75-C76), appropriate phenotype frequencies (C77), genotyping validation (C79), and dramatic transcript reduction (0.3%, C82). The lower germline transmission without preselection (4.8%, C74) contrasts with preselected founders, supporting the value of screening.

result: A donor with single SV40 PA without mutExon was insufficient to stop target gene transcription, as all Cre-injected embryos from kctd10 heterozygote crosses developed normally despite loss of fluorescence, suggesting multiple PA signals or mutExon are necessary for efficient gene disruption.
evaluation: Claims C84-C85 describe negative results from initial donor designs that informed the final strategy. The observation that embryos developed normally despite Po-cassette removal provides important evidence for the necessity of the dual-termination approach (2PA + mutExon), though the data are noted as unpublished.

result: Fin clip junction PCR provides an alternative method for enriching germline transmission events. For tbx5a PoR-NeG screening, 6/48 founders were junction PCR-positive in fin clips, and 2/5 of these showed germline transmission, while 0/20 PCR-negative founders transmitted KI alleles.
evaluation: Claims C90-C96, C156-C159 establish fin clip junction PCR as a viable alternative screening method with quantitative data showing correlation between somatic tissue integration and germline transmission. The 2/5 (40%) success rate in PCR-positive founders versus 0/20 in negative founders (C157-C158) demonstrates practical utility, though lower than embryo preselection.

result: F1 progeny from germline-positive tbx5a KI founders showed more specific and uniform tdTomato expression than mosaic F0 embryos, revealing a clear antero-posterior gradient of tbx5a expression in ventricles (no signal in OFT, highest in AVC) that was scarcely detectable by in situ hybridization.
evaluation: Claims C52-C55 demonstrate the gene-labeling utility of the system with comparative imaging data (Figure 1B-C vs Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,F). The detection of expression gradients not visible by in situ hybridization (C54) validates the superior resolution of fluorescent labeling, though this is a qualitative comparison.

result: A tbx5a indel mutation (tbx5aΔ5) with 5 bp deletion in exon 3 was isolated as a control, showing severe heart and fin defects at 48 hpf in homozygotes, consistent with previous reports of tbx5a loss-of-function mutations.
evaluation: Claims C56-C58 describe generation and validation of a control mutant allele. The phenotype consistency with prior work (Garrity et al., 2002) provides appropriate validation, though this is primarily a methodological control rather than a novel finding.

result: A transgenic line Tg(cmlc2:zCreERT2-2A-ECFP) was generated showing heart-specific expression of inducible CreERT2. After 4-HT treatment, green fluorescent signals were detected in hearts of tbx5aPoR-NeG embryos, demonstrating tissue-specific and temporal control of Cre-induced recombination.
evaluation: Claims C108-C110 demonstrate temporal and spatial control of the geno-tagging system using an inducible Cre line. The detection of green fluorescence specifically in hearts after 4-HT treatment (C109) with no signal in untreated controls (C110) validates the system's controllability, though this is a proof-of-concept rather than extensive characterization.

result: The dual-cassette donor method achieves three levels of genome modification: (i) one-step CKO allele generation, (ii) simultaneous fluorescent labeling of CKO alleles for gene tagging, and (iii) differential labeling of normal vs defective alleles for geno-tagging, enabling discrimination of three genotypes (homozygous normal, heterozygote, homozygous mutant).
evaluation: Claims C136-C138 summarize the demonstrated capabilities of the system. All three levels are supported by experimental data at multiple loci (tbx5a, kctd10, sox10), with clear evidence for each function. This represents an accurate synthesis of the major findings.

result: CRISPR/Cas-induced indel mutations are prone to genetic compensation triggered by premature termination codons. The geno-tagging strategy, which disrupts genes without introducing PTCs, may avoid genetic compensation, while the original PoR-Ne donor with mutExon might trigger compensation.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C11-C12, C142-C143 discuss genetic compensation as motivation and potential advantage of the geno-tagging approach. While the concern about PTC-induced compensation is well-established (C11 with citations), the claims that the geno-tagging strategy avoids compensation (C143) and that the PoR-Ne donor might trigger it (C142) are speculative and not experimentally tested in this study.

result: Multiple polyA signals are more effective for transcription termination. For sox10, 8xPA was used, but this may cause stability issues through repeat reduction or recombination. The authors recommend starting with 2PA and adding more signals if needed based on testing in founder embryos.
evaluation: Claims C119-C120, C145-C149 discuss polyA signal optimization. While the principle that more polyA signals improve termination is cited (C119), the concerns about 8xPA instability (C146-C148) are speculative without experimental evidence. The recommendation (C149) is practical but based on limited comparative data between 2PA and 8xPA designs.

result: There is a strong correlation between efficient germline transmission and correct donor insertion in somatic tissues. Approximately half (10/21) of embryonic stage preselected sox10 founders showed germline transmission.
evaluation: Claims C151-C152, C155 describe the correlation between somatic and germline integration. The quantitative data for sox10 (10/21, ~48%, C155) and tbx5a (5/9, >50%, C153) support this correlation, though the sample sizes are modest and the correlation is not perfect (some PCR-positive founders don't transmit).

result: The dual-cassette donor design provides flexibility for various applications beyond CKO and geno-tagging, including simulating precise mutations, conditional gene rescue, maternal/zygotic analysis, and potential adaptation to other model systems (mice, Drosophila) or medical research.
evaluation: Claims C160-C165 discuss potential future applications of the dual-cassette system. While the flexibility of the design is logical (C160), all specific applications mentioned (C161-C165) are speculative and not experimentally demonstrated. These represent reasonable extrapolations but lack supporting data.

result: The current strategy has limitations: omission of introns and 3'-UTRs may alter gene expression patterns, the approach may not work for genes with alternative splicing, and retention of plasmid backbone sequences might cause DNA methylation. These limitations can potentially be addressed through modified donor designs.
evaluation: Claims C166-C174 acknowledge limitations of the current approach. The omission of introns/UTRs (C167) is a documented design choice, and concerns about expression alterations (C168) and alternative splicing (C171) are reasonable. The plasmid backbone concern (C174) is supported by citation. The suggestions for addressing limitations (C170, C172) are logical but not experimentally validated.

result: Prior to this work, no 'two-in-one' KI strategy combining CKO with fluorescent gene-labeling had been reported, current NHEJ-based methods cannot generate CKO alleles through one-step insertion, and methods for discriminating different alleles of the same gene have not been established.
evaluation: Claims C3, C14-C15, C18, C20-C21, C139 describe gaps in prior work that motivated this study. While these claims about the literature are plausible, they are difficult to verify without comprehensive literature review. Claim C14 cites Su et al. 2017 suggesting some related work exists, and claim C18 cites Burg et al. 2018 about NHEJ limitations, but the absolute statements about what has "not been reported" or "not been established" may be overstated.

result: Background claims about genome editing technologies: CRISPR/Cas systems have revolutionized genome editing, NHEJ-based insertion is more efficient than HR-based strategies in zebrafish, and various gene-trap cassettes can achieve conditional inactivation. The combination of CKO and gene labeling would be useful for zebrafish research.
evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C13, C16-C17, C19, C22, C150 provide background context supported by extensive citations. These are well-established facts in the field rather than novel findings. The utility statement (C22) is reasonable inference based on zebrafish advantages for live imaging.
